title: What is known about 1RB1LA_0LC0RC_1LE1RD_1RE1RC_1LF0LA_---1LE
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1LA_0LC0RC_1LE1RD_1RE1RC_1LF0LA_---1LE.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open, and now provably equivalent to a question about one number sequence. The tape is always A>0 1^p 0 1^q at the sample point. Lean proves the whole map, with exact step counts: odd p: (p, q) → ((p−3)/2, q + (p+5)/2); even p: (p, q) → (3p/2 + q, 1); p = 0: (0, q) → (2, q−1); p = 1 halts. Lean proves that the machine halts from blank tape iff the orbit of (0, 2) under this map reaches p = 1, iff some sample K(p, 1) has p + 3 a power of two, and that a halt, if any, comes after more than 22073 steps (kernel; 280181 by compiled evaluation). Heuristically it never halts.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 20,414 cells have been visited and 20,412 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: exp/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.05). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.53).

claims.title: The odd case of the map
claims.text: K(2k+3, q) reaches K(k, q+k+4) in exactly 2k²+10k+13 steps, for all k, q (k passes of inner_odd by induction, then end_odd); K(0, q+1) → K(2, q) in 7 steps; K(1, q) halts; blank tape reaches K(0, 2) after 7 steps.

claims.title: The even case of the map
claims.text: K(2k+2, q) reaches K(3k+3+q, 1) in exactly q(4k+8)+6k²+22k+15 steps, for all k, q: q passes of inner_even move the block to the right end (even_iter), then an inner induction at the blank (end_loop: each round, end_even and two more inner_even passes, moves two ones of the block out and adds three ones on the left), then end_fin walks back to the left end.

claims.title: The whole map, checked against the machine
claims.text: Before the Lean proof: the map agrees with the machine for every p < 40, 1 ≤ q < 20, and its first 64 samples agree with a direct C run to 6·10<sup>9</sup> steps (K(59806, 1)). Now superseded by the proofs above.

claims.title: 200,000 samples without a halt
claims.text: Iterating the map from K(0, 2): no halt in 200,000 samples; p then has 40,089 bits.

claims.title: Why it should not halt
claims.text: An odd p is halved again and again ((p−3)/2, i.e. p + 3 is halved) until it is even; it reaches 1 only if p + 3 was a power of two (this equivalence is proved). The values of p at the start of these chains grow geometrically, and the chance that a number of size X is 3 less than a power of two is about 1/X, so the expected number of future hits is far below one.

claims.title: The reduction: halting is a question about one orbit
claims.text: With F the map above (F(1, q) = (1, q)) and orbit n = Fn(0, 2): blank tape reaches K(orbit n) after exactly time n steps for every n (reach), and the machine halts from blank tape iff some orbit n has p = 1 (halts_iff), iff some orbit n has q = 1 and p + 3 a power of two (halts_iff_pow2).

claims.title: If it halts, it takes more than 2<sup>2073</sup> steps
claims.text: Any halting run is longer than time n for every n (time_lt_of_halts); Lean's kernel evaluates time 5000 ≥ 22073.

claims.title: If it halts, it takes more than 2<sup>80181</sup> steps
claims.text: The same with time 200,000 ≥ 2<sup>80181</sup>, by compiled evaluation.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Open: by the proved reduction, equivalent to whether the orbit of (0, 2) under F ever produces a sample K(p, 1) with p + 3 a power of two.

explainer.lede: Probably never, but nobody can prove it. The tape is just two blocks of ones; the machine halves the first block when it is odd and multiplies it by 3/2 (plus the second block) when it is even. Lean proves that it stops exactly if the first block ever has length 3 less than a power of two, and not before 2^2073 steps.

facts.text: The whole map and the reduction, proved for all p and q.
A halt, if any, comes later than this.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.05). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.53).
After 109 steps the tape spans 20,414 cells (52 left of the start, 19,739 right), with a density of 1s of 1.0.

The tape (run-length coded, 1^5 is five 1s, C>0 the head in state C on a 0) at some of the last moments the head reached a new cell, cut to 400 characters:

sections.heading: Two blocks of ones
html: Each time the head is at the left end of the tape in state A on a blank cell, the tape is A>0 1^p 0 1^q: two blocks of ones separated by one 0. Call this K(p, q). From blank tape: K(0, 2) at step 7, then K(2, 1), K(4, 1), K(7, 1), K(2, 7), K(10, 1), K(16, 1), K(25, 1), K(11, 16), K(4, 24), K(30, 1), …, K(241, 1), K(119, 124), K(58, 186), K(273, 1).

Between samples the head works on the first block in passes. If p is odd, every pass moves the 0 after the block two cells left and puts one 1 on each side (the left ones pile up at the far left); if p is even, every pass moves the whole block one cell right, eating one 1 of the second block.

sections.heading: Halve when odd, times 3/2 when even
html: Worked example: K(241, 1) has p odd, so the next sample is K(119, 1 + 123) = K(119, 124); 119 is odd: K(58, 124 + 62) = K(58, 186); 58 is even: K(87 + 186, 1) = K(273, 1).

The whole map is proved in Lean for all p and q, each case with its exact step count: an odd p = 2k+3 takes 2k²+10k+13 steps, an even p = 2k+2 takes q(4k+8)+6k²+22k+15 steps. In the even case the block first walks right, eating the second block one 1 per pass; at the blank end it is then taken apart two ones at a time, each round adding three ones on its left, which is where the factor 3/2 comes from.

sections.heading: Only if p + 3 is a power of two
html: Write u = p + 3. The odd rule is u → u/2, so a run of odd values halves u until it is odd. It passes through p = 1 (u = 4), the halting case, exactly when u started as a power of two. Each run of halvings starts right after an even step, at a sample K(p, 1). So: the machine halts iff some sample K(p, 1) has p + 3 a power of two. This equivalence is a Lean theorem (halts_iff_pow2), resting on the proved map: the machine's halting problem is exactly this question about one number sequence.

Those p grow geometrically (200,000 samples reach 40,089 bits), and a random number near X is 3 below a power of two with probability about 1/X, so the expected number of hits is tiny: the machine is probably non-halting. A proof would need to rule out every hit, a Collatz-type statement.

Since every sample of the orbit is proved to be reached at a known step, the orbit also bounds any halt from below: the kernel evaluates the step count of the first 5,000 samples, so if the machine ever halts it does so after more than 22073 steps (280181 with 200,000 samples by compiled code).

summary: Two blocks of ones K(p, q): an odd p is halved ((p−3)/2, the second block absorbing the rest), an even p becomes 3p/2 + q; proved in Lean: it halts iff some p reached with q = 1 has p + 3 a power of two, and not before 2^2073 steps.
